name: Hindutva
info: Hindutva is a Hindu nationalist ideology, formulated by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar in Essentials of Hindutva in 1923, that grounds Indian nationhood in a shared Hindu culture and guides the RSS, the VHP and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

facts.thinkers: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, who gave the word its political meaning; K. B. Hedgewar, founder of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh in 1925; M. S. Golwalkar, his successor at its head; Syama Prasad Mukherjee, founder of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh; Balasaheb Deoras, third head of the RSS; Mohan Bhagwat, its head as of 2026
facts.texts: Chandranath Basu, Hindutva: Hindur Prakrita Itihas (1892), an early use of the word; V. D. Savarkar, Essentials of Hindutva (1923; later retitled Hindutva: Who Is a Hindu?); Savarkar, “Abolition of Caste” (1930) and The Spirit of Hindutva (1935); the Bharatiya Janata Party’s Palampur resolution (1989)
facts.ideas: a Hindu is one who regards India, from the Indus to the seas, as both fatherland and holy land; common nation (rashtra), race (jati) and culture (sanskriti) as the essentials of Hindu identity; Hindutva as distinct from Hinduism the religion; the Hindu nation, Hindu Rashtra; an undivided India, Akhand Bharat; a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens
facts.today: the guiding ideology of the RSS and the Sangh Parivar, among them the Vishva Hindu Parishad and the Bajrang Dal; adopted by the Bharatiya Janata Party in 1989 and pursued in part by Narendra Modi’s governments since 2014; also espoused by the Hindu Mahasabha and the Shiv Sena; networks of groups in the United States, the United Kingdom and elsewhere

t: Savarkar defined a Hindu as one who regards India, from the Indus to the seas, as both fatherland and holy land, and distinguished Hindutva, a national and cultural identity, from Hinduism as a religion.

From the RSS, founded in 1925 after Hedgewar met Savarkar, grew the Sangh Parivar, including the Vishva Hindu Parishad (1964) and the Bharatiya Janata Party (1980), which adopted Hindutva as its ideology in 1989.

Its nature is disputed: some scholars call it fascist or near-fascist, others an extreme conservatism or ethnic nationalism, while the BJP calls it cultural nationalism and not a religious or theocratic concept.
dyk: Savarkar, an atheist, opposed the caste system: under him the Hindu Mahasabha held all-caste dinners in Nagpur and Kanpur, and he gave parents money so that their children of the so-called lower castes would attend school.
ev: Chandranath Basu uses the word in his Bengali book Hindutva: Hindur Prakrita Itihas
Vinayak Damodar Savarkar sets out the ideology in Essentials of Hindutva
K. B. Hedgewar, inspired by Savarkar, founds the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh
The Vishva Hindu Parishad is founded to protect and promote the Hindu religion
The Bharatiya Janata Party is founded
The BJP officially adopts Hindutva as its ideology in the Palampur resolution
The Modi government revokes the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370
Narendra Modi performs the ground-breaking ceremony for the Ram Mandir at Ayodhya

sections.origins:
Hindutva, a neo-Sanskrit word meaning “Hindu-ness”, gained currency among Bengali intellectuals in the colonial era: Chandranath Basu used it in his book of 1892. The historian Prabhu Bapu traces its meaning to the colonial experience, memories of religious wars as the Mughal Empire decayed, Muslim and Christian proselytisation, and a feeling that Hindu traditions were being insulted. According to the sociologist Chetan Bhatt, the forms of Hindu nationalism have roots in the second half of the 19th century, in colonial experience joined with European ideas of nation, race, Aryanism, Orientalism and Romanticism.

Vinayak Damodar Savarkar gave the word its political meaning. Already famous for his account of the Indian Rebellion of 1857, he studied in London between 1906 and 1910, where he worked out his idea of Hindu identity and befriended Indian student groups and others such as Sinn Féin. Arrested for anti-British activity, he submitted several mercy petitions from prison promising loyalty to the crown, and after his release moved away from anti-colonial politics to develop Hindutva.

In 1923 he set out the ideology in Essentials of Hindutva. According to Christophe Jaffrelot he composed it in reaction to the pan-Islamic mobilisation of the Khilafat movement, in which Indian Muslims pledged support to the Ottoman caliph, and his thought reflects a deep hostility to Islam and its followers.
sections.ideas:
For Savarkar the three essentials of Hindutva were a common nation (rashtra), race (jati) and culture (sanskriti). “A Hindu means a person who regards this land of Bharatvarsha, from the Indus to the seas as his Father-Land as well as his Holy-Land”, he wrote. He distinguished Hindutva from Hinduism, describing it as “not a word but a history”, and included Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism as religions of Indian origin. Converts to Christianity or Islam who cherished the shared culture could, in his view, be re-integrated. In Jaffrelot’s reading Savarkar, who declared himself an atheist, minimised religion in favour of an ethnic group with a shared culture and geography, and to him “Muslims were the real enemies, not the British”.

The scholar Chakravarthi Ram-Prasad notes that opponents call it a fundamentalist ideology, while its proponents see it as their right to cherish their religious and cultural traditions; for Savarkar, he argues, “the ultimate category for Hindutva is culture.” Hindutva stresses the territorial unity of India as Akhand Bharat, “Undivided India”, and seeks a Uniform Civil Code under which the same law applies to all citizens whatever their religion. The BJP calls it cultural nationalism and its conception of Indian nationhood, not a religious or theocratic concept. Savarkar opposed hereditary caste, and the RSS heads Balasaheb Deoras and Mohan Bhagwat have called for ending caste discrimination.
sections.spread:
Savarkar’s ideology reached K. B. Hedgewar in Nagpur in 1925; after discussions with Savarkar he founded the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh in September of that year, a paramilitary organisation whose shakhas held physical and martial training and ideological lessons. Under Hedgewar and his successor M. S. Golwalkar the RSS kept out of politics. Savarkar became president of the Hindu Mahasabha in 1937, and Syama Prasad Mukherjee later founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh with the RSS as its political arm.

After Nathuram Godse, a former RSS volunteer, assassinated Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru’s cabinet banned the RSS and arrested more than 200,000 volunteers; according to the political scientist Nandini Deo, the government’s commissions later found the RSS innocent of a role in the killing. The Jan Sangh had limited success in elections from 1952 to 1971. Resistance to Indira Gandhi’s Emergency of 1975 to 1977 brought rapid growth, Jan Sangh leaders such as Atal Bihari Vajpayee and L. K. Advani rose to national prominence, and the Bharatiya Janata Party was founded in April 1980.

The RSS set up the Vishva Hindu Parishad in 1964. In the 1980s the VHP and the BJP drew on a sense of Hindu vulnerability, from killings of Hindus by the Khalistan movement to the Shah Bano case, to advance the Ram Janmabhoomi movement, and the BJP adopted Hindutva in its Palampur resolution of 1989. The RSS founded its first group abroad in Kenya in 1947.
sections.power:
Since the BJP won the general election of 2014, Narendra Modi’s government and BJP state governments have pushed parts of the Hindutva agenda. On 5 August 2019 the Modi administration revoked the limited autonomy of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court; it was accompanied by the deployment of thousands of security forces, the detention of Kashmiri politicians and thousands of civilians, and a years-long lockdown and communications blackout. After a Supreme Court verdict on the disputed site at Ayodhya, Modi performed the ground-breaking ceremony for the Ram Mandir on 5 August 2020, and the temple was completed in January 2024.

Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, all ruled by the BJP, brought in laws against conversion through marriage, aimed at what Hindutva advocates call “love jihad”, which is widely considered an Islamophobic conspiracy theory; the Uttar Pradesh ordinance of 2020 carried sentences of up to 10 years in prison. Many BJP states have also passed laws against cattle slaughter.

Since the mid-2010s there has been a notable increase in violence motivated by Hindutva, particularly against Muslims, perpetrated by or implicating members or alleged members of organisations such as the RSS and Abhinav Bharat, and condoned by BJP politicians. Cow vigilantism has risen since 2014: a Reuters report counted 63 attacks between 2010 and mid-2017, with 28 deaths, 24 of them Muslim, most after Modi took office.
sections.critiques:
Many scholars have pointed out that early Hindutva ideologues were inspired by fascist movements in Italy and Germany, and Marzia Casolari has traced the borrowing. In 1931 B. S. Moonje met Mussolini and wished to copy the fascist youth movement in India. Savarkar endorsed the Nazi persecution of the Jews, likened Indian Muslims to the Jews of Germany, and as late as 1961 spoke favourably of Nazi Germany. Prabhat Patnaik calls Hindutva “almost fascist in the classical sense”. Others dissent: Jaffrelot sees it as an extreme ethnic nationalism differing from fascism in not fusing the movement with its leader and in placing society above the state and race, Chetan Bhatt and Parita Mukta call it “revolutionary conservatism” or “ethnic absolutism”, and Achin Vanaik denies it belongs to the genus of fascism.

Critics of its view of caste include the economist Jean Drèze, who calls the Hindutva project “a lifeboat for the upper castes”, and the Dalit activist Kancha Ilaiah, for whom “Hindutva Is Nothing But Brahminism”. Anthony Parel calls Savarkar’s picture of a self-sufficient Hindu culture “an unhistorical, narcissistic and false account of India’s past”, and Hindutva organisations have been criticised for treating events in Hindu mythology as history. The movement has often been criticised for misusing Hindu religious sentiment to divide people along communal lines and for distorting the inclusive and pluralistic nature of Hinduism for political gain.
sections.legacy:
The contemporary meaning of Hindutva largely derives from Savarkar, as do the nationalism and mass political activity in India since the 1980s. Its legal standing has been argued in the courts. In 1966 the Supreme Court of India held that Hinduism is “impossible to define” and may be described as “a way of life”, and seven rulings of the 1990s, the “Hindutva judgments”, described Hindutva as a “way of life” or “state of mind” rather than a political ideology. The lawyer A. G. Noorani argued that the court “may have brought down the wall separating religion and politics”, and the historian Mukul Kesavan that the judgments lent legitimacy to a sectarian vision of India; in 2016 the court declined to review the 1995 judgment.

Hindutva has been associated with threats and intimidation directed at academics. In 2021 scholars of South Asia in North America published the Hindutva Harassment Field Manual, and the Association for Asian Studies described Hindutva as a “majoritarian ideological doctrine” distinct from Hinduism. Wendy Doniger’s book ceased publication in India after a legal settlement, and the historians Romila Thapar and Audrey Truschke have been targets of attacks and harassment.

Hindutva’s promotion of Hindi, in the slogan “Hindi-Hindu-Hindustan”, alarmed the non-Hindi regions and the demand was put down. A subgenre of Indian pop, Hindutva pop, openly calls for violence against minorities, especially Muslims, though its artists say it promotes truth.

summary: Hindutva is the Hindu nationalist ideology that V. D. Savarkar formulated in 1923, defining Hindus as those who hold India their fatherland and holy land. Carried by the RSS from 1925, adopted by the Bharatiya Janata Party in 1989, it has shaped Indian government since 2014; its proponents call it cultural nationalism, while many scholars compare it to fascism; violence motivated by it, above all against Muslims, has risen since the mid-2010s.
references: Siddharth Varadarajan, Gujarat: The Making of a Tragedy (2002)
V. D. Savarkar, Essentials of Hindutva (1923)
notes: References: the saved article’s Citations, Bibliography and Further reading sections are all empty. The three works are those the article names in its text: Varadarajan’s book (scholarly/journalistic), Savarkar’s own text (a primary source) and the 2021 manual (by a collective of scholars, no author named). Only Varadarajan’s is a secondary work; replace if you prefer.

Violence: written only as the article states and attributes it (the “Hindutva violence” and cow vigilantism sections, Reuters figures, Human Rights Watch left out for length). The 2002 Gujarat riots and the destruction of the Babri Masjid appear in the article only in passing (Verma’s daughter, Drèze), with no account of what happened, so I did not describe them.
The Gandhi assassination and RSS ban are not dated in the article; I left them undated (no event).

“Many scholars have pointed out that early Hindutva ideologues were inspired by fascist movements” is the article’s wording; the lede’s “mutually beneficial relationship with Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany” is not repeated because the article gives no details of it.
Mohan Bhagwat as RSS head “as of 2026” is the article’s phrase.
Karnataka’s anti-conversion law of 2021 was later revoked; I named only Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat as states that passed such laws.
The power section attributes violence to “members or alleged members” and says it was “condoned by BJP politicians”, as the article does (it also says “used as an electoral strategy”, left out).
The 1966 Supreme Court case is Yagnapurushdasji; the 1995 judgment was authored by Justice J. S. Verma (both left unnamed for length).
